title: The Dial-and-Defend answer method
summary: Five moves that turn a design question into a defensible answer: clarify the dials, list options, pick and flip, name failure modes with detection, then state metrics and rollout.
useIf: You face an open design question and need a structure that shows judgement under time pressure.
avoidIf: The question is a factual lookup with one right answer, such as a parameter name.

explain.md: A **dial** is a fact about the situation that changes the best answer: corpus size, update rate, permission model, tenancy, latency target, risk and cost. Interviewers leave dials unspecified on purpose. A strong answer finds them before naming a technology, then defends a choice **for those dials** and says which dial change would flip it.

steps.title: 1. Clarify the dials
steps.md: Ask two to four questions that would change the answer. State assumptions for anything unanswered.

steps.title: 2. List the options
steps.md: Name every sensible option, including the boring baseline to beat.

steps.title: 3. Pick and flip
steps.md: Choose for the stated dials. Say which dial and threshold would flip the choice.

steps.title: 4. Failure modes
steps.md: For the choice, name how it fails and how you would detect it.

steps.title: 5. Metrics and rollout
steps.md: State what you will measure, the threshold that counts as good, and how you ship safely.

explain.md: **Worked example.** Prompt: make an assistant answer questions about information the model never saw. Dials: the corpus is 80,000 tokens, changes monthly, one tenant, p95 latency under 4 seconds, low risk. Options: prompt with the documents (the boring baseline), RAG, fine-tuning. Pick the prompt with caching. Flip: if the corpus outgrows the window or permissions become per user, move to RAG. Failure: answers degrade deep in a long prompt, detected by a golden set with answers placed at different depths. Metrics: groundedness, p95 latency, cost per answered question. Rollout: shadow traffic, then a small cohort.

explain.caption: The dial checklist
head: Dial
Question to ask
Why it moves the answer
rows: Decides prompt, RAG or index design
Who may see what, and how fast does revocation need to apply?
Decides filters, indexes and live checks
What p95 does the user feel?
Decides streaming, caches and model size
What does a wrong answer cost?
What is the budget per task?

explain.title: Say the flip aloud
explain.md: The sentence that separates good from great is the flip: "If the corpus outgrows the window, or permissions become per user, I switch to RAG." It names a dial and a threshold, so the interviewer can test it.

whereToUse: Design interviews for AI engineer and architect roles
Design reviews, where it keeps debate on constraints instead of favourite tools
Written proposals: each section maps to one move
Coaching sessions, where a facilitator scores answers against the five moves
Boss rounds in this guide, which use the same rubric

use: The question names a goal but not the constraints
Several options are plausible and the choice depends on facts you can ask for
You have 3 to 10 minutes to speak
You need to show that you can change your mind for good reasons
avoid: The interviewer asks for one specific fact, so answer it first and then add the method
You already have all the dials stated, so skip move 1 and say so
The prompt is a coding exercise with one correct output
flips: Time is 90 seconds: keep one clarifying question, two options, one flip and one failure mode
Risk is high: spend more of the time on failure modes, detection and human review
The interviewer pushes back with a new constraint: restate it as a dial change and re-run moves 2 to 3

pitfalls.symptom: The answer starts with a product name
pitfalls.cause: The candidate skipped the clarify step
pitfalls.fix: Open with two or three questions about the dials, then state assumptions

pitfalls.symptom: The pick has no flip condition
pitfalls.cause: The candidate treated the choice as universal
pitfalls.fix: End the pick with: if dial X crosses threshold Y, I switch to Z

pitfalls.symptom: Failure modes are generic, such as hallucination
pitfalls.cause: No link between the chosen option and how it breaks
pitfalls.fix: Tie each failure to the option, and add how you would detect it, for example a golden set or a trace alert

pitfalls.symptom: The answer ends at the architecture
pitfalls.cause: Metrics and rollout were treated as optional
pitfalls.fix: Close with metrics, thresholds, shadow traffic and a rollback trigger

scenarios.title: The open design prompt
scenarios.situation: An interviewer says: design an assistant that helps support agents answer customer questions. You have 5 minutes and no other detail.
constraints: The interviewer will answer a few questions
unknowns: How large and how fast-changing is the knowledge?
What is the latency target and the cost of a wrong answer?
scenarios.question: How do you open?

options.name: State assumptions without asking
options.why: Fast, and acceptable when the interviewer declines to answer.
options.tradeoff: You may assume a dial wrongly and defend the wrong design.

options.name: Ask 3 targeted dial questions, state assumptions for the rest, then list options with a baseline
options.why: It shows that the answer depends on facts and it fits the timebox.
options.tradeoff: Uses about 30 seconds that a rival answer would spend on design.

options.name: Start by naming a managed search service and a vector index
options.why: It commits to RAG before knowing size, permissions or latency, so it may be the wrong layer.
options.tradeoff: Naming a stack is right once the dials are known and RAG is the pick.

flips.if: The interviewer says the knowledge is a 30-page handbook
flips.then: Offer a prompt with the handbook as the baseline and show when RAG would replace it.

flips.if: The interviewer says each agent sees only their region's data
flips.then: Lead with permission filters and per-user access in the options.

scenarios.title: High-risk answer in four minutes
scenarios.situation: The prompt is a loan-advice assistant. Wrong answers can cause financial harm and the interviewer says you have four minutes.
unknowns: Is a human in the loop before advice reaches the customer?
scenarios.question: How do you spend the time?

options.name: Spend three minutes on retrieval design
options.why: Retrieval quality matters, but the stated risk puts safety and oversight first.
options.tradeoff: Deep retrieval design is right when risk is low and the question is about search quality.

options.name: Compress moves 1 to 3 into half the time, spend the rest on failure modes, detection, human review and rollout
options.why: In a high-risk domain the interviewer listens for how it fails and how you catch it.
options.tradeoff: The option comparison is shorter, so name the boring baseline in one sentence.

options.name: Give equal time to all five moves
options.tradeoff: Under-weights the high-risk dial, which should earn more time.

flips.if: Risk is low and the topic is internal search
flips.then: Shift time toward options and metrics.

flips.if: The interviewer asks to go deeper on one move
flips.then: Drop the others to one sentence each and go deep there.

scenarios.takeaway: Weight your time by the dial that carries the most risk.

scenarios.title: The interviewer changes a constraint
scenarios.situation: You chose a prompt with cached documents. The interviewer says the corpus is ten times larger and each user sees only some documents.
constraints: The new facts are a size change and a permission change
You must respond in under a minute
unknowns: What does a user's permission set look like?
scenarios.question: What do you say?

options.name: Throw away the design and start again from the beginning
options.tradeoff: It wastes the baseline, metrics and failure thinking you already did.

options.name: Defend the prompt design with a larger window
options.why: Per-user permissions and size break the single prompt design.
options.tradeoff: Defending your pick is right only when the new fact does not cross your stated threshold.

options.name: Restate both as dial changes, switch to RAG with access filters, and explain what you keep
options.why: You show that you reason from dials and that your earlier flip condition predicted this.
options.tradeoff: You must be ready to cover ingestion and ACL capture next.

flips.if: The new facts do not cross your stated flip threshold
flips.then: Keep the choice and show the arithmetic.
Add a live permission check on sensitive hits.

scenarios.takeaway: Treat pushback as a dial change, not as an attack.

quiz.q: Put the five moves in order.
items: Pick and say what would flip it
Name failure modes and how to detect them
quiz.explain: You cannot list good options before the dials are known, and you cannot name failure modes before you pick an option. Metrics and rollout close the answer.

quiz.q: Which sentence is a proper flip condition?
options: If the corpus outgrows the window or permissions become per user, I switch to RAG
It depends on the use case
quiz.explain: A flip names a dial and a threshold and the option you switch to. The other statements are opinions, an extra option or a hedge with no condition.

quiz.q: Which are dials you would ask about for a new assistant?
options: The colour of the user interface
quiz.explain: Update rate, permissions and latency each change which option wins. The interface colour does not affect the architecture choice.

flashcards.front: List the five moves of Dial-and-Defend.
flashcards.back: Clarify the dials, list the options (with the boring baseline), pick and flip, name failure modes with detection, then metrics and rollout.

flashcards.front: What makes a flip condition good?
flashcards.back: It names a dial, a threshold and the option you switch to, for example: if permissions become per user, I move to RAG.

flashcards.front: Name the seven dials in the checklist.
flashcards.back: Corpus, update rate, permissions, tenancy, latency, risk and cost.
